> 知人者智，自知者明。勝人者有力，自勝者強.

Four chapters have been pulling inward: the world cannot be forced (29), force cannot be relied on (30, 31), names have to know where to stop (32).

By this point the external objects are cleared. One step further in, and only one thing is left — yourself.

So chapter 33 changes rulers. It measures the practice itself, in four pairs:

知人／自知, 勝人／自勝, 知足／強行, 不失其所／死而不亡.

Eight lines, four pairs. In every pair, the first half is what people are currently chasing. The second half is what the chapter is after.

## 智 and 明

知人者智 — knowing others is 智. 智 is the ability to figure things out: to read a person, to see through a situation, to say clearly what is going on.

自知者明 — knowing oneself is 明. 明 is the word from chapter 16: not cleverness but illumination.

The difference is the direction of the light. 智 is a light you point outward; it illuminates the object. 明 is the state of being lit — the light is not yours to aim, because it is not a beam at all.

That is why knowing others is easier and cheaper: the object is at a distance, and you can be wrong about it without consequence for a while. Knowing yourself has no distance, and no place to hide the error.

## 力 and 強

勝人者有力 — beating others is 力: strength, the physical capacity to prevail. 力 is what your body has.

自勝者強 — conquering yourself is 強. And 強 is the character from chapter 30's warning: 物壯則老.

強 is not "greater force." It is the drawn bow — 弓 with 疆: tension held, a structure under load that does not collapse.

So 自勝 is not a bigger fight against yourself. It is the capacity to hold tension without being deformed by it. Which is why it is harder than beating someone: the opponent is inside the perimeter.

## 知足者富

知足者富 — the one who knows sufficiency is rich.

富 is not "having a lot." In its old sense 富 is 備 — complete, provisioned, having what is needed for the task at hand.

So the line does not say "be content with little." It says: richness is the condition of being adequately provisioned, and the person who can recognize that condition is rich regardless of the amount.

The failure it addresses is the one where abundance cannot register as abundance, because the measure keeps moving.

## 強行者有志

強行者有志 — the one who 強行 has 志.

強行 here is not "force your way." It is 勉力 — exerting effort deliberately, toward what is inward.

志 is the direction held in the will — not ambition, but the orientation that keeps effort pointed at the same place over time.

The location matters: 強行 is paired with 知足, not with 勝人. Effort spent outward is 力; effort spent inward is 志.

## 不失其所者久

The one who does not lose his place lasts.

所 is the place — in the old sense, the position that is one's own, the post one holds. Not a location, but the ground one's function stands on.

久 is duration without erosion: the same 久 as chapter 16's 道乃久.

## 死而不亡者壽

> 死而不亡者壽.

Dies and does not perish: this is 壽.

壽 normally means long life. Here it is redefined: what does not perish is not the body, and the line does not say what it is. It leaves the term and lets the reader locate it.

The chapter's four pairs are all versions of one axis — 向外求合, or 向內守和. 知人, 勝人, and outward effort are the first; 自知, 自勝, sufficiency, and holding one's place are the second.

## A test

For each of the four, note which half you spend your days on. Most people are excellent at the first half of all four pairs and have never measured the second.
